newsitem.title: GEORGIA: Georgian route for Azeri oil cheaper-AIOC official.
newsitem.headline: Georgian route for Azeri oil cheaper-AIOC official.

text.p: A proposed pipeline to transport oil through Georgia from a consortium developing Azerbaijan's Caspian reserves would be cheaper than an alternative route through Russia, a consortium official said on Tuesday.
Ex-Soviet Georgia and Russia have been competing for the route, which would carry oil to world markets via Black Sea ports, and the lucrative transit fees the pipeline could bring.

"The capital cost of this pipeline has been calculated and the cheapest capital cost would be using a Baku-Supsa route," said John W. Hollins, Senior Vice President of the Azerbaijan International Operating Company (AIOC).
Baku is the capital of Azerbaijan and Supsa is on Georgia's Black Sea Coast.

AIOC, a 13-member consortium, signed an $8 billion deal in 1994 with the Azeri government to develop three offshore fields. The consortium is led by British Petroleum Plc and Norway's Den norse stats oljeselskap (Statoil).

First crude oil from the project is scheduled to come on stream later this year. AIOC intends to use two existing pipelines to get early oil to Black Sea outlets, one through Russia and one through ex-Soviet Georgia.

The pipelines do not have the combined capacity to handle later peak production from the project. AIOC says it will announce where it will build the new pipeline needed to accomodate full production later this year.
AIOC expects early oil output of around 100,000 barrels per day, rising to 700,000 to 800,000 bpd by 2010.

Other options being considered for carrying Caspian oil to world markets include a link to the Mediterranean via Ceyhan in Turkey and routes bypassing the Bosphorous, including a Balkan link between Bourgas in Bulgaria and Alexandroupolis in Greece.
Bob Moore, Senior Vice President of the Georgian Pipeline Company, which represents the AIOC in Georgia, said the republic had "a good chance" of securing the new pipeline.
"Georgia is on the map in terms of international oil transportation," he said.
Georgia will announce the winner of a tender for a feasibility study on a pipeline crossing its territory by the start of May, officials of the state oil company said.
Nikolai Gvazava, coordinator for the Georgian International Oil Corporation (GIOC), told Reuters that seven foreign firms had put in bids for the project.

He said they were Caffney, Cline and Associates of the United Kingdom, Gulf Interstate Engineering of the U.S., John Brown E&C of the U.S., Ukraine's Ukragasproekt, SNC-Lavalin International Inc. of Canada, and Tebodin Consultants and Engineering of the Netherlands.
"All of these companies have very good experience in the field," Gvazava told Reuters.
The World Bank last week approved a $1.4 million long-term credit to Georgia to help pay for the study.
